video_title: The A.I. Trade "Is In Its Final Inning" - Next Comes A Recession | Porter Stansberry
gist: Porter Stansberry (Porter & Company) tells Adam Taggart the AI capex boom is in its final inning: as funding shifts from equity to debt, the bond market will cut off CoreWeave, then Oracle, then a hyperscaler, forcing ~75% capex cuts, a 2027 recession with rapid white-collar job losses, Nvidia revenue down ~50% and a Nasdaq drawdown. He positions via 'yellow light' defensive allocation (50% cash / 25% blue chips / 25% gold streamers and Bitcoin for retirees), his systematic 'honeycomb' equity strategy (top-ROC, long-lived companies in six best industries plus gold royalties), and Weyerhaeuser timber as a hedge.

themes.theme: AI capex bust: bond market as tripwire

insights.claim: Porter Stansberry believes the AI trade is in its final inning and that there will be an AI bust before the end of 2027, modeled on the 1999 fiber-optic build-out where heavy capex drove the price of bandwidth to virtually zero.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Positions for a late-cycle AI infrastructure unwind rather than a new leg up.
insights.quote: I think that the AI trade is in its final inning, and that before the end of 2027 there will be an AI bust.

insights.claim: Capex booms always die when the bond market says no more; AI funding has shifted from equity to debt this year and next year's planned ~$500B of debt funding will not happen, ending the circular financing.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Watch AI-related credit spreads and debt issuance capacity as the key leading indicator for the AI trade.
insights.quote: they always die when eventually the bond market says no more

insights.claim: Stansberry's sequencing: the bond market has already cut off CoreWeave, will cut off Oracle next, then eventually a hyperscaler, at which point hyperscalers will cut capex by about 75%, all within the next 12 months.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Oracle credit/funding access is the next domino to monitor; hyperscaler capex guides are the endgame.
insights.quote: The bond market has already cut off CoreWeave. Um it'll cut off Oracle next.

insights.claim: Stansberry calls CoreWeave a zero, expects Oracle to crash (not something you'll want to own), and expects Nvidia revenue to fall by about 50%, none of which he thinks is priced in, implying a big Nasdaq drawdown given its AI weighting.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Explicit short/avoid list: CoreWeave, Oracle; downside risk to Nvidia and Nasdaq-heavy portfolios.
insights.quote: particularly I think that CoreWeave is a zero

insights.claim: The internet boom ended about nine months after the Fed began raising rates in 1999; Stansberry says the Fed raised rates in September for the first time in three years, meaning the tightening cycle that will end the AI bubble has begun.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Implies a mid-2027 window for the AI bust if the 1999 analog holds.
insights.quote: the internet boom, it ended nine months after the Fed started raising rates in 1999

insights.claim: AI capex has been about a third of US economic growth over the past 12 months; its collapse would take a large share of GDP growth off the table, moderate commodity and tech-services demand, liquidate weaker tech business models and cause a recession next year.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Cyclical/commodity exposure is also at risk from an AI capex reversal, not just tech.
insights.quote: That's about a third of our entire economy in the past 12 months.

insights.claim: Stansberry uses the 10-year Treasury yield as his signal: over 5% is 'yellow light mode' and over 6% is 'red light mode', because rising cost of capital is what ends every capex boom; he is already in yellow light mode.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: A concrete risk-off trigger level to track: 10-year at 5% and 6%.
insights.quote: once the 10-year yield got over 5% it was going to be what I call yellow light mode

insights.claim: Infrastructure builders rarely capture the profits of a technology build-out ('Chinese restaurant metaphor': the second or third owner makes the money); Adams Express never owned railroad track but leased space, took railroad stock as payment, became the largest shareholder in the Pennsylvania Railroad and Union Pacific and sold at the 1929 peak.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Favor businesses that use cheap infrastructure over those that fund it.
insights.quote: The guy who builds the Chinese restaurant is never the guy who makes the money from the Chinese restaurant.

insights.claim: Stansberry is optimistic long-term on Anthropic because it rents its compute, passes costs to users and benefits as compute prices fall, while compute builders such as Oracle, CoreWeave and to some extent Microsoft, Amazon and Meta face a much tougher future (though he is not suggesting buying the IPO).
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Long AI application/model users, cautious on compute owners.
insights.quote: I'm actually optimistic about the long term for something like Anthropic, which rents all of its compute

insights.claim: Unlike fiber or rail, AI chips are essentially worthless within a decade, so there will be little 'dark compute' (demand for compute is endlessly elastic like electricity), but owning compute will be a poor investment because there is no moat: each new Nvidia chip renders prior builds uncompetitive and pushes compute prices toward zero.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Compute will be fully used but commoditized; value accrues to users, not owners of GPUs.
insights.quote: I don't think there's anybody out there who says that in 10 years an H100 AI chip is going to be worth anything

insights.claim: Because compute must be continually replaced, Stansberry thinks an AI bust will be much worse than the railroad bust; with five-plus providers (SpaceX, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, CoreWeave, Oracle) offering the same compute, competition will compete away all the profit.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Expect margin compression across GPU cloud providers.
insights.quote: if there are five companies, SpaceX, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, CoreWeave, Oracle, and they're all offering you compute, who makes any money?

insights.claim: Going from ~$50B a year to ~$1 trillion a year in tech capex dramatically raises the risk, and unforeseen efficiency breakthroughs (like packetized voice in the internet era) could expand effective capacity and further undercut compute pricing.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Efficiency breakthroughs are a downside risk to compute pricing and GPU demand.

themes.theme: AI agents and white-collar job destruction

insights.claim: Stansberry says he will never hire another human, after replacing a departed top biotech analyst (Rhodes scholar, ex-Tiger Management) with seven AI agents that track 12 scientific development paths daily for roughly $100 a day in credits.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Real-world evidence of agentic AI substituting for high-skill analyst labor at low cost.
insights.quote: I'm not ever hiring another human ever again.

insights.claim: Stansberry predicts white-collar unemployment will rise very rapidly in a 2027 recession and that professional jobs (lawyers, accountants, doctors) will be destroyed, with none existing in 10 years; he sees no point getting a law, accounting or medical degree.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Bearish for professional-services labor and related spending; consumer-spending risk from white-collar layoffs.
insights.quote: this is going to absolutely destroy the entire professional class in the United States

insights.claim: Stansberry says there is no reason today for the ~3 million US long-haul truck drivers to have jobs given existing technology; conversion to driverless trucks could be done in 12 months but market forces will likely take 6-12 years.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Long-dated tailwind for autonomous trucking, headwind for trucking labor.

insights.claim: Unlike Adam Taggart, who worries about Keynes-style technological displacement outpacing redeployment, Stansberry rejects the concern, wants displacement as fast as possible, opposes UBI, and argues the real risk is government responses (citing Smoot-Hawley turning the 1920s productivity boom into the Great Depression, and today's global tariffs).
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Policy reaction (tariffs, transfers) is the main macro risk in Stansberry's view, not AI itself.
insights.quote: The problem is always what the government does in response to that crisis.

insights.claim: Stansberry finds AI drafting unpublishable 'slop' and strategy ideas hit-or-miss (two brilliant out of ten), likening it to a 160-IQ intern without real-world understanding, and expects audiences to get very good at detecting AI-written content.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Human-authored, trusted content retains a premium; pure AI content businesses risk commoditization.
insights.quote: like having an intern that has 160 IQ

insights.claim: Facing the commoditization of information by AI (readers can 'do it themselves on Claude'), Stansberry is shifting his research business from email/literary to in-person community: 8-12 subscriber trips a year and a planned investing-focused community in The Villages, Florida.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Information businesses must pivot to community/trust to keep pricing power.
insights.quote: very shortly, people are not going to be willing to pay just for information

insights.claim: Stansberry sees healthcare/biotech as AI's ultimate application, noting the first purely AI-designed antibody is starting clinical trials, and expects transformative change over the next decade.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: AI-enabled drug discovery is a long-term area of focus.
insights.quote: the very first pure AI designed antibody is now starting clinical trials

insights.claim: In 'yellow light mode' Stansberry recommends retirees following his permanent-portfolio approach sell financial stocks and hold 50% cash, 25% ultra-high-quality blue chips (e.g., Eli Lilly, Coca-Cola, Microsoft) and 25% gold streaming companies and Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: A concrete defensive allocation for an AI-bust/recession scenario; exit financials.
insights.quote: they should have already sold their financial stocks

insights.claim: Gold and Bitcoin have been correlated to the tech boom, but Stansberry expects them (along with Coca-Cola, Philip Morris and Hershey's) to protect wealth over time when the boom ends, citing gold in Q4 2008.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Expect near-term correlation but longer-term hedge value from gold/Bitcoin.

insights.claim: Stansberry's ETF PCPP (Porter & Company Permanent Portfolio) modifies Harry Browne's permanent portfolio by using 20 'Lindy' stocks instead of the S&P 500 and holding bonds via property & casualty insurers that actively manage duration; he says it is up about 15% this year, aiming for equity-like returns at about half the volatility.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Option for retirees seeking lower-volatility exposure; P&C insurers as a bond proxy.
insights.quote: That approach will give you equity-like returns, but with about half of the volatility of the stock market.

insights.claim: The honeycomb is a fully invested equity strategy: take the six best-performing industries for investors over 50 years (including beverages, tobacco, compute, P&C insurance and aerospace), own the top two companies in each by three-year return on capital, add the top gold streamer, ~7% per position, rebalanced once each June after annual filings.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: A systematic, low-turnover quality strategy investors can replicate.
insights.quote: you ask yourself, what are the very best performing industries for investors?

insights.claim: Return on capital is measured per industry: ROIC for a company like Coca-Cola, growth in book value plus dividends for a P&C insurer like WR Berkley; companies must also be among the oldest in their industry (100 years, or 60 years for aerospace and 30 for compute).
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Longevity filter screens for proven survivors as a quality edge.
insights.quote: the key rule is that the company has to be one of the oldest in its industry

insights.claim: Stansberry says the honeycomb has never had a losing June-to-June year since 1998, averaging about 16% annually over 28 years; its worst drawdown was just over 30% in about six weeks during COVID, and it was up 7% June-to-June through 2008.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Backtested resilience claim; expect volatility but historically positive annual results.
insights.quote: you've never had a losing year from June to June

insights.claim: In 2001, the last big tech wreck, the honeycomb was up 52% largely because Royal Gold rose 300%, with tobacco, beverages and aerospace also doing well, which is why Stansberry bets it won't lose money June-to-June even in a 2027 recession.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Gold royalty and defensive staples have historically offset tech busts.
insights.quote: in 2001 which was the last big tech wreck the honeycomb was up 52% for the year

insights.claim: The gold slot is almost always Royal Gold or Franco-Nevada, occasionally Wheaton Precious Metals; this June's compute picks were ASML and Logitech (with Apple third), though Stansberry personally swapped Logitech for Apple.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Named current holdings in a systematic quality screen.

insights.claim: Stansberry claims seven industries gives the best Sharpe ratio, the efficient frontier between diversification and concentration, and that a 30-stock portfolio would just be 'buying the Dow' without alpha.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Concentration of ~14 stocks at ~7% each is his sweet spot.

insights.claim: Stansberry calls trees the most resilient asset, compounding 2-4% annually regardless of the Fed or markets; Weyerhaeuser (WY), with an 11-million-acre US forest, yields about 4.5% versus ~4% margin borrowing at Interactive Brokers, letting him own the forest 'essentially for free', and trades well under half replacement cost.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Weyerhaeuser as a hedge against economic catastrophe and a long on a future US housing boom.
insights.quote: So, I can own the very finest forest in the world essentially for free.

insights.claim: Stansberry expects another US building boom because of housing needs and notes lumber is increasingly used for 10-15 story buildings, supporting long-term timber demand.
insights.speaker: Porter Stansberry
insights.so_what: Structural demand tailwind for timber owners.
